source_ref: Novak, Malinakova, Mikoska, van Dijk, Dechterenko, Ptacek & Tavel (2021), 'Psychometric Analysis of the Czech Version of the Toronto Empathy Questionnaire', IJERPH 18:5343, CC BY, doi:10.3390/ijerph18105343; OSF deposit osf.io/z85cv. This table is the study's DSES block. Scale length and anchors from the paper's Methods. Item wording and the instruction text from Underwood & Teresi (2002) as reproduced in full, numbered, and with Underwood's explicit permission, in a CC BY paper (Europe PMC PMC11970868, Appendix A).
note: ALL FIFTEEN ITEMS SHIP, BECAUSE THE CZECH RENUMBERING IS PUBLISHED. The Czech 15-item DSES is Underwood's 16 items minus item 5 ('I find comfort in my religion or spirituality', dropped for r=.92 with item 4) -- Malinakova et al. 2018, Ceskoslovenska psychologie 62 Suppl.1. So Czech position n maps to Underwood 1-4, 6-16 in order. IRW already relied on that renumbering once, for CV_OASIS_ODSIS_PPE_Novak_2020_DSES in batch_024, from the same research group. IT WAS NOT TAKEN ON TRUST. Three pins derived here independently all agree with it: the code suffixes on SPIRIT_12_ALTR and SPIRIT_13_PRIJ name altruism and prijeti (acceptance), and the renumbering puts Underwood's 'selfless caring' and 'accept others' at exactly 12 and 13; and SPIRIT_15 carries four response levels where every other item carries six, where the renumbering puts Underwood's closeness question. A fourth check tests all fifteen at once -- see the verification evidence. THE SCALE DIRECTION HAD TO BE SETTLED FROM DATA BECAUSE THE SOURCES CONTRADICT EACH OTHER. The source paper states 'Many times a day' (1) to 'Never or almost never' (6) and then says 'a higher score indicates a higher degree of spirituality', which cannot both be true. Two further papers from the same group state the anchors in the opposite order. The live data decides it: the SCBCS compassion mean, whose direction the same paper states unambiguously, correlates -0.317 with the DSES mean, and the same paper reports a positive association between compassion and spirituality -- which holds only if a higher DSES value means less spiritual experience. So the anchors ship as printed and the interpretive clause is the erroneous half. SPIRIT_15 correlates +0.680 with the other fourteen, so it runs the same way, meaning its four labels are reversed relative to Underwood's printed order. The live codes carry three source typos -- SIPRIT_8 and SPRIT_14 for SPIRIT_8 and SPIRIT_14 -- reproduced verbatim because item is the join key. Wording is Underwood's English; the administered Czech is not published in the deposit or the paper.
public_note: The Daily Spiritual Experience Scale as used in a Czech study, 15 items. The Czech version is the original 16-item scale minus one item, and the published renumbering is what lets each code be matched to a question here. READ THE DIRECTION CAREFULLY: 1 means 'Many times a day' and 6 means 'Never or almost never', so a HIGHER number means LESS frequent spiritual experience. The source paper states these anchors but also says a higher score means more spirituality, which is not consistent with them; the data agrees with the anchors. The last item asks how close you feel to God on a four-point scale running the same way, 1 closest. The item text is Underwood's English original -- the study administered a Czech version whose wording is not published, so what is shown is a rendering rather than what respondents read. Three item codes carry typos from the source data and are left as they are so they still match the response table.

source_ref: Küster, Baker & Krumhuber (2022), 'PDSTD - The Portsmouth Dynamic Spontaneous Tears Database', Behavior Research Methods 54:2678, CC BY, doi:10.3758/s13428-021-01752-w; OSF deposit osf.io/uyjeg, file 'Observer ratings.csv'. note: THE CODE IS THE SOURCE COLUMN HEADER, so there is no mapping step; what needed establishing was which of the two rating blocks each item belongs to, and the data proves that outright. The paper describes two blocks: four 100-point VAS ratings (negative valence, positive valence, arousal, genuineness; 0 'not at all', 100 'very much') and seven discrete-emotion sliders whose ratings 'had to sum up to 100%'. That constraint is a hard arithmetic test, and it holds on every one of the 2,184 rating occasions for the seven emotions while the four VAS ratings range freely to 301. So section_id is confirmed without reading a single item name. ITEM_TEXT IS THE PAPER'S DESCRIPTION OF EACH DIMENSION, NOT A SCREEN TRANSCRIPT, and is written as such ('the degree of perceived negative valence', 'the extent to which anger is reliably expressed in the face'). The paper does not print the literal on-screen prompts. The published definitions of arousal and genuineness ship verbatim in section_prompt rather than being folded into the items. option_text carries the two labelled VAS endpoints only; the emotion sliders are percentages with no labels. resp is continuous 0-100, so the table ships one row per observed value per item, the same treatment the numeric items get in the chile tables. NOTE WHAT id MEANS: id is the stimulus VIDEO and rater is the observer, so anything grouping by id is grouping by clip.
public_note: Eleven ratings that observers gave to each video clip in a database of spontaneous weeping. Four are 100-point scales for negative valence, positive valence, arousal and genuineness, running from 0 'not at all' to 100 'very much'; the study's own definitions of arousal and genuineness are given with them. The other seven ask how strongly each of seven emotions is expressed in the face, as percentages that had to add up to 100 across the seven. The wording shown is the study's description of each rating rather than the literal text observers saw on screen. Note that id here identifies the video being rated, not a person; the observer is in rater.

source_ref: Yeatman, Tang, Donnelly, Yablonski, Ramamurthy, Karipidis et al. (2021), 'Rapid online assessment of reading ability', Scientific Reports 11:6396, CC BY, doi:10.1038/s41598-021-85907-x. note: THE ITEM CODE IS THE STIMULUS ITSELF, so item_text is a transcription rather than a label: the code is the word or pseudoword that was flashed on screen for 350 ms. The live data carries realpseudo per item, and the paper fixes the buttons outright: 'Participants pressed right for a real word or left for a pseudoword.' So each item ships two option rows, each carrying the resp it scores (1 for the correct button, 0 for the other), its raw_resp key name, and the item's correct_response. ONE SOURCE IS GONE: the GitHub repository data/lexical_roar.R cites (github.com/yeatmanlab/LexicalDecision) now returns 404, so the stimulus list could not be re-read to confirm this is the paper's version-1 list rather than a later revision. Since the codes ARE the stimuli this does not affect the item text, only the provenance of the list.
public_note: A lexical decision task: 500 stimuli, 250 real words and 250 pseudowords, each flashed for 350 milliseconds. The item code is the stimulus itself. Participants pressed the right arrow for a real word and the left arrow for a pseudoword, and resp records whether that judgement was correct, so each stimulus is listed twice -- once for the button that was correct for it and once for the button that was not.
